newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set for marathon beef battle as BSE fears grow.
newsitem.headline: EU set for marathon beef battle as BSE fears grow.

text.p: European Union farm ministers start a three-day meeting on Monday to thrash out measures to aid farmers and revive markets reeling from more scientific evidence that mad cow disease could spread to people.

The evidence, announced by British scientists on Wednesday, prompted EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler to stress the importance of maintaining a seven-month-old global ban on beef exports from Britain.

But officials said British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg and Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth were expected to say there was no cause for fresh concern during private talks with Fischler at the EU farm council in Luxembourg.

Since March, Britain has taken measures to protect public health on the assumption of a link between the cattle disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), and it human equivalent, Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease (CJD), the officials added.
The two ministers were also likely to discuss a possible exemption of certified BSE-free British herds from the ban.
But officials said progress was stalled until after EU scientists rule in mid-November on British research casting doubt on whether an extra cull of cattle was needed.
Britain used the research to shelve the cull, involving up to 147,000 cattle, which was a pre-condition for easing the ban.

For his part, Fischler will use other new data to make a fresh attempt on Monday to win the support of reluctant ministers, notably the Spanish, to agree to a total ban on suspect sheep and cattle parts in human and farm animal food.
The data showed that BSE could also be transmitted to humans in the form of CJD, by eating meat from infected sheep.

The need for EU measures was highlighted on Friday when Germany said it planned to ban the import and use of selected beef and sheep products from France and Britain as part of measures to protect German consumers against mad cow disease.
Germany also strongly opposes a package of measures put forward by the EU's executive Commission to aid livestock producers and remove beef surpluses.
Since March, beef consumption has fallen by around 15 percent across the continent and the EU has bought some 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef for storage to prevent a price collapse.

The package is made up of short-term measures, such as extra purchases of unwanted beef, including meat from younger animals, and a premium to slaughter new born calves. It also has longer measures, such as livestock investment grants.
"It's inefficient, imbalanced and financed in the wrong way," Germany's State Secretary for Agriculture, Franz-Josef Feiter, told visiting reporters in Bonn.

Germany, which favours intensive production, has proposed a different approach giving incentives to beef producers to slaughter animals earlier and at lighter weights, selling the meat on to the market rather than into intervention stores.
But France, where angry livestock producers paralysed traffic in the centre of the country on Friday, wants more aid for traditional farmers, especially with suckler cows.

"Member states are divided on almost every issue on this part of the agenda and it is hard to see how the impasse will be resolved," one diplomat said, noting huge opposition to a plan to fund the package by slashing aid to cereals farmers.
As a result diplomats said only a mini-package of the most urgent measures may be agreed at the meeting.
